top_cited_works.title: Bubble-induced skin-friction drag reduction and the abrupt transition to air-layer drag reduction
top_cited_works.abstract: To investigate the phenomena of skin-friction drag reduction in a turbulent boundary layer (TBL) at large scales and high Reynolds numbers, a set of experiments has been conducted at the US Navy's William B. Morgan Large Cavitation Channel (LCC). Drag reduction was achieved by injecting gas (air) from a line source through the wall of a nearly zero-pressure-gradient TBL that formed on a flat-plate test model that was either hydraulically smooth or fully rough. Two distinct drag-reduction phenomena were investigated; bubble drag reduction (BDR) and air-layer drag reduction (ALDR). The streamwise distribution of skin-friction drag reduction was monitored with six skin-friction balances at downstream-distance-based Reynolds numbers to 220 million and at test speeds to 20.0ms −1 . Near-wall bulk void fraction was measured at twelve streamwise locations with impedance probes, and near-wall (0 < Y < 5mm) bubble populations were estimated with a bubble imaging system. The instrument suite was used to investigate the scaling of BDR and the requirements necessary to achieve ALDR. top_cited_works.title: On the scaling of air layer drag reduction
top_cited_works.abstract: Abstract Air-induced drag reduction was investigated on a 12.9 m long flat plate test model at a free stream speed of $6. 3~\mathrm{m} ~{\mathrm{s} }^{- 1} $ . Measurements of the local skin friction, phase velocity profiles (liquid and gas) and void fraction profiles were acquired at downstream distances to 11.5 m, which yielded downstream-distance-based Reynolds numbers above 80 million. Air was injected within the boundary layer behind a 13 mm backward facing step (BFS) while the incoming boundary layer was perturbed with vortex generators in various configurations immediately upstream of the BFS. Measurements confirmed that air layer drag reduction (ALDR) is sensitive to upstream disturbances, but a clean boundary layer separation line (i.e. the BFS) reduces such sensitivity. Empirical scaling of the experimental data was investigated for: (a) the critical air flux required to establish ALDR; (b) void fraction profiles; and (c) the interfacial velocity profiles. A scaling of the critical air flux for ALDR was developed from balancing shear-induced lift forces and buoyancy forces on a single bubble within a shear flow. top_cited_works.title: Using cross correlations of turbulent flow-induced ambient vibrations to estimate the structural impulse response. Application to structural health monitoring
top_cited_works.venue: The Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
top_cited_works.abstract: It has been demonstrated theoretically and experimentally that an estimate of the impulse response (or Green's function) between two receivers can be obtained from the cross correlation of diffuse wave fields at these two receivers in various environments and frequency ranges: ultrasonics, civil engineering, underwater acoustics, and seismology. This result provides a means for structural monitoring using ambient structure-borne noise only, without the use of active sources. This paper presents experimental results obtained from flow-induced random vibration data recorded by pairs of accelerometers mounted within a flat plate or hydrofoil in the test section of the U.S. Navy's William B. Morgan Large Cavitation Channel. The experiments were conducted at high Reynolds number (Re > 50 million) with the primary excitation source being turbulent boundary layer pressure fluctuations on the upper and lower surfaces of the plate or foil. Identical deterministic time signatures emerge from the noise cross-correlation function computed via robust and simple processing of noise measured on different days by a pair of passive sensors. recent_works.title: Wind Noise Mitigation of Infrasound Sensor Payloads on High Altitude Balloons
recent_works.abstract: A major limitation of recording infrasound sources via ground-based sensors is wind noise. An approach that mitigates this limitation is the use of balloon-based sensors. Heliotropes, a type of high-altitude solar-powered balloon, float within the lower stratosphere and are regularly used to study infrasound sources due to the minimal relative speed between the air and the balloon (i.e., low wind). However, to determine the direction of arrival for a signal, there must be at least two sensors with a separation comparable to the wavelength. The separation between the balloon and the sensors result can result in higher relative wind speeds compared to the balloon since the sensors are being pulled towed by the balloon. The increased wind noise can obscure infrasound signals of interest. This has motivated the current study aimed at identifying a compact, lightweight infrasound windscreen that can be deployed on high-altitude balloons. Variations of a previous design, termed SunFoam, are evaluated with ground and flight testing. This includes a flight where the use of the SunFoam windscreen reduced the noise floor allowing for the detection of microbaroms.

recent_works.title: Experimental Analysis of Surface-Pressure–Driven Far-Field Noise in Impinging Jet Flows
recent_works.abstract: This study presents an experimental investigation of the aeroacoustic characteristics of subsonic impinging jets interacting with normal and inclined plates for acoustic Mach numbers Ma=0.48, 0.67, and 0.86. Simultaneous far-field acoustic measurements and near-field surface-pressure measurements were conducted to quantify how plate inclination and axial placement modify sound generation and radiation. The far-field spectra show that the noise is dominated by turbulent mixing without evidence of screech tones or broadband shock-associated noise. recent_works.title: Demonstration of the Use of NSGA-II for Optimization of Sparse Acoustic Arrays
recent_works.abstract: Passive acoustic sensing with arrays has applications in many fields, including atmospheric monitoring of low frequency sounds (i.e., infrasound). Beamforming of array signals to gain spatial information about the signal is common, but the performance is often degraded due to limited resources (e.g., number of sensors, array size). Such sparse arrays create ambiguities due to reduced resolution and spatial aliasing. While previous work has focused on either maximizing array resolution or minimizing spatial aliasing, the current study demonstrates how evolutionary algorithms can be utilized to identify array configurations that optimize for both properties. The non-dominated sorting genetic algorithm II (NSGA-II) was used with the beamwidth and maximum sidelobe level as the fitness functions to iteratively identify a group of optimized synthesized array configurations. This group is termed a Pareto-front and is optimized such that one fitness function cannot be improved without a decrease in the other.
